title: Asking questions that open doors
description: The right question, asked gently, can turn a closed answer into a real conversation.

body.heading: Start wide, not narrow
paragraphs: Some questions can only be answered with a shrug. “Was school okay?” usually earns an “okay” back. A wider question — “What was the best part of today?” or “Who made you laugh?” — gives the other person somewhere to go.
Wide questions do not demand a performance. They simply leave more doors open, and the other person can choose which one to walk through, or none of them.

body.heading: Ask one, then wait
paragraphs: A good question needs a little silence after it. If you fill every pause with guesses — “Was it maths? The test? Tom?” — the other person stops searching their own mind and just waits for you to finish.
Waiting is a small act of respect. It says: your answer is worth a few seconds of quiet.

body.heading: Follow the thread they offer
paragraphs: When someone answers, pick up the detail they chose, not the one you expected. If they mention the bus ride instead of the exam, ask about the bus ride. People open up along the paths they pick themselves.
You can always return to the exam later. Conversations are not checklists; they are more like gardens, growing where the light already is.

takeaway: Ask one wide question, wait through the pause, and follow the thread the other person offers.
